extracted.intended_audience: reading researchers, discourse analysts, journalism editors, and educators interested in text comprehension
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how the organization, ordering, and linguistic choices in news narratives (inverted-pyramid newspaper stories) affect readability and comprehension, and comparing those choices with alternative narrative organizations. Useful for analyzing or revising news copy for comprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing as a structural cue
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph boundaries should mark meaningful discourse units; superficial paragraphing (many short paragraphs that do not correspond to distinct units) fails to impose significant structure on the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AP article has 18 paragraphs but only 27 sentences, so paragraphing does not much improve organization. If paragraphs do not represent natural topic or structural units, they will not help readers see connections among facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macrostructure simplicity (fewer, coherent higher-level units)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensible narrative is organized into a small number of larger discourse units (macrostructure) that together give a logically reconstructable account of the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare macrostructures: fabricated accounts (grant proposal, Sheila, Reporter) have 5–6 macro-units that exhaustively cover the incident; the AP story produces many more superficial subdivisions, making it feel oddly organized from a reader's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of presentation of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequence in which facts are presented should support readers' ability to integrate them; ordering convenient to editors (e.g., mixing chronology and topical facts) may be inconvenient for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables comparing sentence-orderings demonstrate that the AP story's order is greatly out of sequence relative to chronological or purpose-driven narrations. Reordering toward a reader-oriented chronology or logically progressive sequence improves comprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted-pyramid vs chronological narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Inverted-pyramid organization (most 'newsworthy' facts first, least important last) differs from chronological narrative structure and can obscure event relations when readers expect a chronological account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AP account follows inverted-pyramid principles suited to skimming, whereas chronological narratives (resume + detailed chronology) make genesis, motivations, and causality clearer for deep comprehension. Choice of structure should reflect communicative goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of connectives to make relations explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit connectives (then, because, but, as a result, in particular, etc.) clarify relationships among facts—temporal, causal, contrastive—and aid comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical comparison shows the AP account has far fewer connectives per sentence than the fabricated accounts (Table 5). Increasing connective density makes relevance relations explicit and reduces inferential load on readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of irrelevant details
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate or clearly contextualize details that do not contribute to the reader's reasonable interpretation of the event (e.g., gratuitous color details), because they distract and obscure structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the color of a scarf or exact policeman wording appears irrelevant in the AP story; unless such details are tied to an interpretive point (e.g., evidence of infiltration), they increase noise and hinder comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing redundancy that doesn't add information
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundant reporting of the same information (e.g., repeating police commander’s exact words or quoting slogans that restate the lead) should be avoided unless it provides new evidence or perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AP account contains redundancies (police phrasing, repeated sign wording) that do not advance understanding. Redundancy is acceptable only when it adds a distinct function (tone, attribution, contrast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on reader inference and skimming
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories often depend on readers to skim and to infer relations among facts; this strategy reduces effort for skim-readers but raises comprehension demands for careful readers, novices, or children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The modern news story is suited to the skimmer; while this supports quick consumption, it can thwart deep understanding by readers who do not automatically integrate isolated facts. Consider audience when deciding how much to rely on inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence length and syntactic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Average sentence length, range, and syntactic composition affect readability; short sentences alone do not guarantee comprehension—connective density and syntactic signaling matter too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 5 shows differences in average words per sentence and ranges among the accounts: AP's shorter sentences but lower connective/verb ratios suggest that brevity without explicit linking reduces comprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and sub-goals shaping organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's communicative goal (e.g., academic exposition, eyewitness account, brief news summary) determines which facts are highlighted, their order, and what relations are made explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Professor, Sheila, and Reporter versions each have different goals (research illustration, eyewitness telling, conversational report) and these goals produce different organizational choices; thus identify purpose before organizing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and coherence of structural units
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many small structural units at the same level (many short paragraphs or sentence clusters) can create a sense of fragmentation; a coherent narrative uses units whose scope and relations are clearly signaled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP story's many subdivisions (11+ for 27 sentences) contrast with other accounts' fewer, more exhaustive units. Group related sentences into coherent larger units and signal their relations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit signaling of causal/temporal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Make temporal and causal connections explicit rather than leaving them to inference; this includes placing genesis/motivation early or clearly linking causes to consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant proposal, Sheila, and Reporter accounts give a brief resumé then chronological detail; the AP story often buries genesis or mixes it, making causal lines hard to follow. Use connective phrases and ordering to indicate causality/temporality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present background/context before consequences when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often comprehend events better if relevant background or context that explains motives or significance is provided before or alongside consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Professor's account highlights causes and the contrast between protestor and police accounts early; for comprehension-sensitive audiences, foregrounding context reduces inference load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious use of quotations and reported speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations should contribute distinct information (attribution, voice, evidence). Overuse or verbatim repetition of reported speech can introduce redundancy and ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the AP article, multiple paraphrases/quotes of police denials and protestor claims create repetition without clarifying relations. Use quotes to add perspective only when they supply new, interpretable content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid textual conventions that teach readers to expect nonconnected facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting and stylistic norms (short sentences, lack of paragraphing, relations inexplicit) in texts aimed at beginning readers or habitual skimmers can prevent development of expectations about connections among ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report hypothesizes that exposure to such norms (in news or beginning-reader texts) may lead some readers, especially children, not to learn to expect connection among ideas and thus to fail to see connections even in better-written texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: skimmability vs deep comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choices that increase skimmability (leading with most newsworthy facts, terse paragraphs) often reduce the explicit signaling of relations and thus deep comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should balance the need for quick scanning by typical newspaper readers against the potential costs for readers who require more explicit structure (students, children, non-experts). Explicit marking and optional expanded versions can help.
